The central question is: when a speculative decoding system generates a draft sequence that diverges from the target model's verification output, how does the resulting prefix invalidation cascade through the KV cache, and what does that cost at runtime? The naive picture — "rejected tokens just get discarded" — misses that KV cache implementations (paged, prefix-sharing, radix-tree-based) have already allocated and possibly shared physical memory blocks for those draft continuations; invalidating a divergence point doesn't free that memory atomically, it triggers a reclamation pipeline that competes with live allocation for new prefill. The expert worry is specifically about the asymmetry between allocation speed and reclamation speed: under high-throughput serving with many concurrent speculative sequences, rejected suffixes create a fragmentation pattern where large contiguous logical sequences are backed by physically non-contiguous, partially-freed block chains — subsequent requests that need long contiguous prefix caches can't reuse these fragments efficiently even after reclamation nominally completes. Worse, in systems using radix-tree prefix sharing (e.g., vLLM's prefix cache), a draft sequence that shares a prefix with many live requests means the invalidation decision is non-trivial: you can't evict the shared trunk just because one speculative branch was rejected, so the rejected suffix blocks linger in a limbo state until reference counts drop, spiking memory pressure precisely when the system is under load. The beginner assumes speculative decoding's KV overhead is bounded by the draft model's extra compute; the expert knows the actual latency budget is often dominated by the interaction between draft-induced fragmentation and the block allocator's inability to reclaim fast enough to prevent stalls on the next accepted-token prefill.

The determinant of fragmentation type is the alignment between draft sequence length and block granularity: if a speculative suffix spans K tokens and the block size is B tokens (vLLM defaults to 16 tokens/block), a rejection at position j within a block leaves (B − j mod B) slots allocated but unused — pure internal fragmentation — whereas a rejection that frees whole blocks but leaves them physically scattered across the allocator's free list produces external fragmentation when subsequent requests need long contiguous logical sequences backed by physically adjacent blocks for efficient memory access. Internal fragmentation is structurally bounded — worst case is (B−1) wasted tokens per rejected sequence, which at B=16 and even hundreds of concurrent speculative sequences amounts to a few MB — but external fragmentation is unbounded in principle because it depends on the interleaving history of allocations and frees across all concurrent requests. The harder recovery problem is unambiguously external fragmentation: reclaiming internal waste only requires finishing or evicting the owning sequence, but resolving external fragmentation requires either compaction (copying live KV blocks to consolidate free space, which is catastrophically expensive at inference time since it invalidates physical pointers cached in attention kernels) or accepting that free memory is effectively stranded. Under sustained high-rejection-rate speculative decoding — Leviathan et al. (2023) report acceptance rates as low as 0.6 on adversarial distributions — the free list evolves into a pathological checkerboard: short-lived draft suffixes are constantly allocated and freed at offsets that interleave with long-lived prompt prefixes, and the allocator can't coalesce because the surviving blocks are still live. Systems like vLLM's block manager mitigate this with a "watermark" free-block threshold that preemptively swaps requests before the allocator stalls, but this converts fragmentation-induced stalls into preemption-induced recompute, trading memory pressure for latency spikes on the evicted request's re-prefill. The practical signal experts watch is the ratio of num_free_blocks to num_used_blocks reported by the block manager: when this ratio stays high but new allocation requests still stall, that's the fingerprint of external fragmentation — plenty of free memory in aggregate, none of it in useful contiguous runs for the block sizes the incoming requests need.

The minimum per-node state required is a triple: a reference count tracking how many live sequences currently hold the node as part of their active prefix, a tombstone bit set when a speculative descendant invalidation marks the node as logically dead but physically retained, and a last-access timestamp (or LRU generation counter) used to order eviction candidates once the reference count drops to zero. The reference count alone is insufficient because it only tracks current users — a node whose refcount just hit zero might still be the shared trunk for a dozen sequences that will re-enter it on their next decode step (common in batched serving of similar prompts), so premature eviction forces expensive re-prefill; the tombstone bit defers that decision, marking the node as "evict when convenient" rather than "evict immediately." The timestamp resolves the tombstone queue under memory pressure: when the allocator needs blocks, it scans tombstoned nodes in LRU order rather than evicting arbitrary live nodes, which is exactly the policy implemented in vLLM's prefix_cache branch where evictor.py maintains a priority queue keyed on last-access time over zero-refcount blocks. Without the tombstone bit, the only safe policy is to defer all eviction until refcount==0 AND no pending speculative runs reference the subtree — but tracking "pending speculative runs" requires either a second reference count (one for live sequences, one for in-flight draft sequences) or a generation number that increments on each speculative rollback, both of which add per-node write pressure on the hot decode path. SGLang's radix attention (Zheng et al., 2024) handles this with a two-level scheme: inner nodes carry only a refcount and a "pinned" flag set during active speculative expansion, while leaf nodes additionally carry a validity token that gets invalidated on draft rejection, allowing the tree to defer inner-node eviction without walking the full subtree on every rollback. The critical invariant the system must enforce is that a node's physical KV blocks must not be returned to the free list while either (a) its refcount is nonzero or (b) its tombstone is set and a speculative run still holds a pointer into its subtree — violating condition (b) is the source of the use-after-free class of bugs that appear under high concurrency when the allocator reclaims tombstoned blocks faster than the draft model's verification loop can complete.

The race window opens the moment the draft device increments a block's reference count and begins transferring KV tensors over NVLink or PCIe, but before the target device has verified the draft tokens and sent an acknowledgment back to the cache coordinator: if a concurrent eviction decision on the coordinator reads the refcount between the draft's allocation increment and the target's verification-triggered pin, it sees an apparently safe eviction candidate and reclaims the block, causing the target's verification kernel to read stale or zeroed KV data mid-transfer. This is structurally identical to the TOCTOU (time-of-check to time-of-use) problem in filesystem page caches, and the naive fix — holding a coordinator lock across the entire draft-transfer-verify round trip — serializes all speculative sequences through a single mutex, destroying the throughput advantage of disaggregation entirely. The correct primitive is a epoch-based hazard pointer scheme adapted from lock-free memory reclamation (Fraser 2004, Herlihy & Shavit): each speculative sequence registers a hazard pointer to the set of block IDs it currently holds before initiating transfer, the coordinator's eviction path checks all registered hazard pointers before reclaiming any block, and reclamation only proceeds for blocks not appearing in any live hazard set — this makes the eviction path O(S·B) in the number of sequences S and blocks per sequence B, but completely off the critical decode path. DistServe (Zhong et al., 2024) sidesteps this by treating prefill and decode as pipeline stages with explicit token-passing rather than shared KV memory, which eliminates the race at the cost of full KV retransfer on every draft-target handoff; true disaggregated speculative serving (as prototyped in systems like Medusa with remote draft heads) instead needs a lightweight pending-transfer bitmap per block, a single bit set on draft allocation and cleared only on verified acknowledgment or explicit rollback, with the eviction path skipping any block whose pending bit is set. The synchronization cost then reduces to one atomic test-and-set per block per speculative step on the draft side and one atomic clear on the target side — both can be implemented as CUDA atomic operations on a host-pinned bitmap, keeping the critical path to a single PCIe round-trip for the bitmap update rather than a full coordinator RPC. The residual danger experts watch for is acknowledgment loss under target-side rejection: if the target rejects draft tokens and the rollback message is dropped or delayed, the pending bit stays set indefinitely, the block is never evicted, and the cache silently leaks — robust implementations therefore pair the pending bit with a per-block timeout counter, triggering forced rollback and refcount decrement if the verification acknowledgment doesn't arrive within a configurable deadline (typically 2–3× the expected draft-verify round-trip latency).

response:
Standard free-list pressure models used in continuous batching schedulers (e.g., vLLM's block manager) estimate memory consumption as mean_acceptance_rate × draft_length × batch_size × block_size, treating all sequences as exchangeable — but this mean-field approximation catastrophically underestimates peak block demand when per-sequence acceptance rates have high variance, because the maximum concurrent block footprint is driven by the high-acceptance tail, not the mean. Concretely, if half your batch has acceptance rate 0.9 (long verified suffixes retained, many blocks pinned) and half has rate 0.3 (frequent rejections, high churn but low steady-state pinning), the mean is 0.6 but the high-acceptance sequences hold blocks for O(draft_length) steps while the low-acceptance sequences create rapid allocation-free cycles that fragment the free list — the combined effect is worse than a homogeneous batch at either extreme because fragmentation from the low-acceptance sequences degrades contiguous block availability precisely when the high-acceptance sequences need to extend their pinned prefixes. This variance-induced distortion means the scheduler's watermark threshold — the free-block count below which it preempts requests — needs to be set not against mean expected usage but against the 95th-percentile block footprint, which for a realistic heterogeneous batch can be 1.4–1.8× the mean estimate based on empirical distributions reported in the Sarathi-Serve paper (Agrawal et al., 2024) for mixed-length workloads. The admission control implication is that naive FCFS admission (accept requests until the watermark is hit) becomes unstable under heterogeneous acceptance rates: a burst of high-acceptance-rate sequences admitted together can push block usage past the watermark mid-batch, triggering cascading preemptions that cause re-prefill latency spikes for already-running sequences, which is strictly worse than having rejected the burst at the gate. The correct policy is variance-aware admission control: each incoming request should carry an estimated acceptance rate (derivable cheaply from a lightweight draft-model probe or from historical per-prompt-type statistics), and the scheduler should maintain a running estimate of the second moment of block demand across the live batch, rejecting or queuing new requests when adding them would push the predicted 95th-percentile footprint above the watermark even if mean footprint remains safe. A subtler implication is that sequences with low but highly variable acceptance rates (e.g., code generation prompts where acceptance is bursty — long accepted runs followed by sudden divergence) are more dangerous to admit than sequences with equivalently low but stable acceptance rates, because their block demand is autocorrelated, meaning a single bad speculative step can spike demand by a full draft_length worth of blocks before the scheduler's next admission-control evaluation cycle.

The minimum sufficient state is a triple per sequence: a sliding-window acceptance rate estimate (e.g., exponential moving average with decay α≈0.9 over the last 8–16 speculative steps), a residual tracking the signed difference between predicted and observed block allocations at each step, and a residual variance accumulator that maintains a running estimate of how noisy that residual has been recently. The residual alone detects bias (systematic over- or under-prediction) but not the onset of a distribution shift that hasn't yet moved the EMA — the residual variance accumulator catches the increase in prediction noise that precedes a bias shift, because prompt distribution changes first manifest as higher step-to-step variability in acceptance outcomes before the mean shifts enough to move the EMA, a pattern well-documented in online changepoint detection literature (Adams & MacKay, 2007, BOCPD). Concretely, the scheduler should compute a CUSUM statistic over the per-step residuals: at each decode step, accumulate S_t = max(0, S_{t-1} + (predicted_blocks - actual_blocks) - slack) where slack is a small tolerance (~0.5 blocks), and trigger a staleness alarm when S_t exceeds a threshold h (typically set to produce one false alarm per 500 steps in stationary conditions) — this detects upward drift in block consumption (the dangerous direction for watermark violations) with a detection lag of roughly 3–5 steps at a 20% shift in true acceptance rate, compared to 15–20 steps for a pure EMA. Without the CUSUM or equivalent sequential test, the EMA's lag means the scheduler doesn't register a distribution shift until the watermark has already been breached by several steps, converting a detectable early-warning signal into a reactive preemption event. The staleness alarm should trigger not an immediate preemption but a conservative re-estimation step: freeze admission of new sequences for one full speculative round, observe actual vs. predicted block delta across all live sequences, refit the EMA with a higher learning rate (α≈0.5) for 4–8 steps to fast-track convergence, then restore normal α — this costs at most one round-trip latency of admission delay (~5–20ms at typical draft speeds) in exchange for avoiding a watermark violation that would cascade into multi-sequence preemption and re-prefill. The critical insight that beginners miss is that the staleness detection problem is asymmetric: over-estimating block demand (predicting low acceptance when actual is high) wastes admission capacity but is safe, while under-estimating (predicting high acceptance when actual diverges and blocks churn faster) causes watermark violations, so the CUSUM threshold h should be tuned to be hair-trigger on the under-estimation side and tolerant on the over-estimation side — an asymmetric loss function that standard EMA-only approaches cannot express.

The optimal preemption ordering is fundamentally different under internal versus external fragmentation, and conflating them is the primary source of suboptimal recovery in production schedulers. Under internal fragmentation dominance — where waste is localized within partially-filled blocks owned by specific sequences — the correct priority is to preempt sequences with the highest ratio of wasted-to-used slots within their allocated blocks, because evicting these sequences returns the most net usable memory per sequence killed; concretely, a sequence that has allocated 10 blocks but only filled 6 tokens in its final block wastes 10/16 of that block, and preempting it returns a full clean block to the free list, whereas preempting a sequence whose blocks are all fully packed returns the same physical memory but at higher re-prefill cost per recovered byte. Under external fragmentation dominance — where the free list is checkerboarded and new allocations stall despite sufficient aggregate free blocks — preempting by wasted-slot ratio is nearly useless, because the problem isn't total free memory but contiguity; here the correct heuristic is to preempt sequences whose allocated blocks are most physically scattered (highest block-address entropy across their allocation), because evicting a sequence whose blocks happen to be clustered in one memory region releases a contiguous run that the allocator can immediately satisfy large requests from, while evicting a scattered sequence releases the same block count but in fragments that don't resolve the contiguity deficit. vLLM's current preemption policy (evict the sequence with the most allocated blocks, i.e., longest sequence first) is a reasonable proxy under internal fragmentation but actively counterproductive under external fragmentation — the longest sequence often has the most scattered blocks precisely because it was allocated incrementally over many steps when the free list was already fragmented, so evicting it returns many blocks but in the worst possible physical layout. The practical implementation requires the scheduler to maintain a per-sequence block-address spread metric (e.g., max minus min physical block index, or standard deviation of block addresses) updated lazily at each allocation step, and at preemption time, sort candidates by a weighted score: λ × (wasted_slots / total_slots) + (1-λ) × (1 / address_spread) where λ is set high (~0.8) when internal fragmentation dominates and low (~0.2) when external dominates, with the dominant type inferred from the ratio of free-block count to allocation-stall rate observed in the preceding re-estimation window. The deeper insight is that the CUSUM alarm context itself carries fragmentation-type signal: if the alarm fired because actual blocks allocated exceeded prediction (sequences consuming more blocks than expected, implying high acceptance rates and long pinned suffixes), external fragmentation is likely dominant because long sequences accumulate scattered allocations; if the alarm fired because block churn rate exceeded prediction (rapid alloc-free cycles from low acceptance), internal fragmentation is more likely because short draft suffixes leave partial blocks.

Yes, this regime exists and is analytically characterizable: draft-length reduction is strictly cheaper than preemption when the marginal block savings from shortening the draft exceeds the expected re-prefill cost amortized over the sequence's remaining lifetime. Formally, let γ be the acceptance rate, d the current draft length, d' the reduced draft length, L the current sequence length in tokens, and C_prefill the per-token prefill cost; the expected blocks freed by reducing draft length is (d - d') × γ × (1/B) blocks per step (since only accepted tokens stay pinned), while the expected re-prefill cost if a preemption were triggered instead is L × C_prefill paid once but amortized over the expected remaining decode steps R, giving amortized cost L × C_prefill / R per step — draft reduction is preferable when (d - d') × γ / B > 0 recovers enough blocks to avoid preemption entirely, which reduces to checking whether the block deficit Δ satisfies Δ ≤ (d - d') × γ × N_high / B where N_high is the count of high-acceptance sequences eligible for draft reduction. The crossover condition sharpens when you account for the throughput penalty of draft reduction: shortening from d to d' tokens reduces expected tokens generated per step from d × γ to d' × γ, a fractional throughput loss of (d - d')/d, so the full trade-off is throughput_loss_cost × remaining_steps versus re_prefill_cost × preemption_probability, and draft reduction wins when remaining steps are few (sequence nearly done, re-prefill amortization period is short) or when the sequence is long (high re-prefill cost makes preemption expensive). Empirically, Miao et al. (2024) in SpecInfer show that reducing draft length from 5 to 3 tokens recovers approximately 15–20% of peak block usage for high-acceptance sequences with γ≥0.8, at a throughput cost of roughly 8–12% — a favorable trade when the alternative is preempting a sequence of length L≥2048 tokens whose re-prefill at typical A100 prefill throughput (~10k tokens/sec) costs 200ms of dead latency. The practical scheduler implementation should treat draft length as a continuous control variable rather than a binary preempt/continue decision, reducing d by 1 token at a time for the highest-acceptance sequences when the block deficit is small (Δ < 10 blocks) and only escalating to preemption when the deficit is large enough that even d'=1 (single-token drafting, effectively greedy) doesn't close the gap — this gives a graceful degradation curve rather than a cliff-edge preemption event. The regime where draft reduction is never preferable is when γ is low (≤0.3) for the candidate sequences, because low acceptance means pinned blocks are already minimal and shortening the draft saves almost no memory while still paying the throughput penalty; in this regime the sequences are already behaving nearly like non-speculative decoding, and preempting one of them is cheaper than degrading the entire batch's draft efficiency.
